item.title: Progress WS_FTP Server: unauthenticated CVSS 10.0 flaw can expose admin credentials; fixed in 2025.0.4 and 2024.0.7
item.description: Progress, as CVE numbering authority, published on 2026-10-29 CVE-2026-84295, an improper-authentication flaw in WS_FTP Server on Windows that could let an unauthenticated remote attacker reach administrative credentials (CVSS 3.1 10.0), together with an unauthenticated command injection under certain configurations (CVE-2026-90865, 9.0) and an access-control flaw in the Web Admin console (CVE-2026-90867, 8.1). Builds before 2024.0.7 and 2025.0.4 are affected, and CSIRT Italia counts 6 critical and 3 high flaws in the release and says Progress will issue no patch for unsupported versions. No source reports exploitation, and CISA's catalog holds no 2026 WS_FTP flaw, though a 2023 flaw in the same product is listed with known ransomware use.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-84295 +2NATOA2

CVE-2026-84295, Progress WS_FTP Server: an unauthenticated remote authentication flaw can expose administrative credentials (CVSS 10.0), with two more unauthenticated flaws, fixed in 2025.0.4 and 2024.0.7; no exploitation found

Progress, as CNA, published CVE-2026-84295 on 2026-10-29: improper authentication in WS_FTP Server on Windows that "could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to access sensitive information, including administrative credentials"; its CVSS 3.1 vector is network, low complexity, no privileges and no user interaction, scored 10.0, and the record names no component or endpoint (ENISA EUVD, 2026-10-29). Two further flaws carry an unauthenticated vector with high attack complexity: CVE-2026-90865, an OS command injection that could allow command execution with elevated privileges under certain configurations (9.0) (ENISA EUVD, 2026-10-29), and CVE-2026-90867, improper access control in the Web Admin console that could expose administrative functionality to remote authentication attempts (8.1) (ENISA EUVD, 2026-10-29). CSIRT Italia counts 6 critical and 3 high flaws in the release, of types including authentication bypass, remote code execution and arbitrary file read and write (CSIRT Italia, 2026-10-30).

The record for CVE-2026-84295 names versions before 2024.0.6 and 2025.0.3 as affected (ENISA EUVD, 2026-10-29), and the records for the other two name versions before 2024.0.7 and 2025.0.4 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-10-29), so 2024.0.7 or 2025.0.4 is the build to reach. CSIRT Italia lists 2025.0.3 (10.0.3) and 2024.0.6 (9.0.6) and earlier as affected and says that for unsupported versions the vendor will not release a workaround or patch (translated from Italian) (CSIRT Italia, 2026-10-30). No source reports exploitation: CISA's catalog holds no 2026 WS_FTP flaw, although CVE-2023-40044 in the same product has been listed since 2023-10-05 with known ransomware use (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-30).

Exposure
Any WS_FTP Server on Windows below 2024.0.7 or 2025.0.4; CSIRT Italia describes it as a secure file-transfer server used within organisations and with external partners, so instances reachable from partner or public networks come first (CSIRT Italia, 2026-10-30). The records name no component for the authentication flaw, so no configuration is known to make an instance safe.
Detection
No source publishes an indicator. For an instance that was reachable before the fix, the records to review are the web-server logs of the Web Admin console and the file-transfer server's own logons for administrator access from unfamiliar addresses, and process creation by the service or its web worker, since CVE-2026-90865 is command execution (an inference from the described flaw).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade to 2024.0.7 or 2025.0.4, partner-facing instances first, and rotate the administrator credentials afterwards, because the upgrade does not change credentials an attacker already read; take an instance on an unsupported branch off the network or migrate it.

item.title: Microsoft: Teams help-desk vishing into Quick Assist ended in AD CS certificates for privileged accounts and a DC
item.description: Microsoft Threat Intelligence describes two human-operated intrusions, not attributed to any actor, in which an external Teams contact impersonating help-desk staff got a user to open Quick Assist, after which the operator staged a portable runtime and used Active Directory Certificate Services to reach privileged identities: a template open to ESC1 issued certificates for privileged accounts and DCSync followed within seconds, and in the second case PetitPotam was relayed to AD CS Web Enrollment (ESC8) for a certificate for a domain controller account. An issued certificate stays valid after a password reset or a reimage of the first workstation, and in the first case one privileged account excluded from automated containment stayed usable and was used to copy data to an external SFTP destination.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Teams help-desk impersonation to domain-controller identity: Microsoft traces two intrusions from a Quick Assist session to AD CS ESC1 certificates with DCSync, and to PetitPotam relayed to ESC8 Web Enrollment

Microsoft Threat Intelligence describes two human-operated intrusions, not attributed to any threat actor, that began with an external Teams contact (across the broader activity Microsoft saw organisation-themed tenant names and support-style display names) who persuaded a user to open Quick Assist and read out the connection code; the activity did not exploit a Teams vulnerability. In the session the operator placed an archive in Downloads, extracted it into a newly created KB-prefixed folder under the user profile and started the payload with a portable Python, JavaScript or Java runtime, which ran host and network discovery and assessed AD CS (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-10-30).

In the first case a certificate template open to ESC1, where the requester supplies the identity, produced certificates for three privileged accounts, and about 90 minutes later for eight more after a second wave against 16 users; DCSync began within seconds of obtaining one privileged certificate. Defender's automated disruption blocked more than 1,000 SMB attempts, but a privileged account excluded from automated response stayed usable, reached a file server and ran a renamed Rclone that copied a share to an external SFTP destination (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-10-30). In the second case the operator used PetitPotam to make a domain controller authenticate to the attacker's host, relayed that NTLM authentication to an AD CS Web Enrollment endpoint, obtained a certificate from the Domain Controller template and used it for PKINIT to get a ticket-granting ticket for the controller's account; Defender raised ESC8 alerts and the customer isolated the workstation (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-10-30).

Exposure
A forest with an enterprise CA whose authentication-capable templates accept requester-supplied identity with broad enrollment rights (ESC1), or whose Web Enrollment or Certificate Enrollment Web Service endpoints lack HTTPS and Extended Protection (ESC8), where Teams accepts external chats and calls and users can start Quick Assist; Defender for Identity's AD CS posture assessments, or an inventory of /certsrv endpoints and template permissions, shows the first two (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-10-30).
Detection
New external Teams contacts from help-desk-themed tenants; in process telemetry, a portable runtime started from a freshly created KB-prefixed folder under the user profile after a remote-support session; in CA records, certificate requests and issuances correlated by requester, subject alternative name and template with the first authentication using the certificate; and a domain controller account authenticating to Web Enrollment from a device that is not that controller, which Microsoft calls a strong pivot (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-10-30). After containment, revoke the unauthorized certificates and assess issued Kerberos tickets separately; a password reset and a reimage of the first workstation leave both in place.

Triage: a help-desk Quick Assist session is routine; what separates this one is an external-tenant initiator with no matching ticket and an interpreter runtime launched from a newly created user-writable folder rather than a managed install path.

Defender takeaway
Require HTTPS and Extended Protection on every enrollment web endpoint, drop the ones nobody needs, review authentication-capable templates and require approval where enrollment is broad, and enable the Certification Services audit subcategory and CA audit filter; limit Teams external access and restrict remote-support tools to approved ones. Treat a containment exclusion as an incident decision with a manual compensating step, because in the first case the one excluded privileged account was the route to the file server (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-10-30).

item.title: Cursor marketplace served a trojanised Claude Code extension for 11 hours; uninstalling leaves the SSH backdoor
item.description: Between about 09:27 and 20:35 UTC on 2026-10-29 the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace served a modified copy of Anthropic's Claude Code extension, versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for macOS and Windows, that appends an attacker's SSH key to authorized_keys, tries to enable SSH and open a reverse tunnel, and installs persistence that outlives the extension. Coding errors made the SSH step fail on most standard-user hosts, so Cursor and Sophos say the attacker could not log in there, but the key, the persistence and a host report were still written. Anthropic told Microsoft its systems were not compromised, and no source says how the attacker published under Anthropic's name.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB1

Cursor marketplace: a tampered Claude Code extension (versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313) planted an SSH key, a reverse tunnel and persistence for about eleven hours on 2026-10-29; uninstalling it does not remove the persistence

Between about 2:27am PT and 1:35pm PT on 2026-10-29 (09:27 to 20:35 UTC) a maliciously modified copy of Anthropic's Claude Code extension, versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for macOS and Windows, was served from the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace; Cursor removed it, shut the marketplace down briefly, rotated its keys, rebuilt it and had the hosting provider take the attacker's server offline (Cursor, 2026-10-29). Anthropic told Microsoft its systems were not compromised and that it did not build the package, and Microsoft confirms the packages were never published to the Visual Studio Marketplace or npm (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-10-30). How the attacker published under Anthropic's name is not disclosed in any source read. Cursor estimates up to 5,000 affected users (Sophos X-Ops, 2026-10-30).

The injected loader runs when the extension module loads. It reports host and user data (hostname, username, operating system, home and working directories, the configured Git email, environment-variable names and public IP address), appends an attacker-controlled SSH public key to authorized_keys, tries to enable the local SSH service and open a reverse SSH tunnel, and installs persistence outside the extension: a LaunchAgent on macOS, and on Windows a scheduled task that asks to run as SYSTEM with a Startup-folder fallback, with background scripts retrying the tunnel about every 60 seconds (Cursor, 2026-10-29). Microsoft's analysis adds a user crontab entry for Linux (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-10-30). Because of coding errors the step that enables SSH fails unless Cursor was started with administrator privileges, so on most hosts the attacker could not log in through the tunnel, but the key, the persistence and the host report still happened (Cursor, 2026-10-29).

Exposure
Any macOS or Windows host on which Cursor installed or auto-updated Anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 inside the window; the code also carries Linux routines though Cursor names only macOS and Windows packages (heise online, 2026-10-30). Extension-install telemetry shows the version. NCSC Switzerland carried the incident on 2026-10-30 but places the backdoored extension on Open VSX and says Anthropic pulled versions from npm and the VS Code marketplace (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-30); Microsoft says the packages never reached the Visual Studio Marketplace or npm, and Cursor and Phorion name the Cursor marketplace, so the entry follows them.
Detection
In process-creation telemetry, an editor's extension host starting ssh or autossh with remote port forwarding and no command; in file-write telemetry, an editor process modifying authorized_keys; and, shortly after an extension update, a new LaunchAgent, scheduled task, Startup-folder script or @reboot crontab entry named after system-monitoring components. Phorion advises matching the attacker key's fingerprint rather than the comment string it carries (Phorion, 2026-10-30). Removing the extension does not remove the persistence scripts, which keep running (Cursor, 2026-10-29).

Triage: a running SSH process is not proof the attacker got in, since both ends must allow the connection (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-10-30); administrators run tunnels too, and what separates this one is an editor extension as the parent process and persistence written to user-writable locations rather than a managed service.

Defender takeaway
Treat a host that ran either version as backdoored whether or not the tunnel connected: remove the key, the persistence and the tunnel processes, rebuild where compromise cannot be excluded, and rotate credentials reachable from it. heise reports a cleaned release, with 2.1.314 as the minimum to install (heise online, 2026-10-30).

item.title: PHP2Shell hits Broadcom endpoint-security servers: App Control 8.12.2 or 8.13.2; SEPM fix builds unconfirmed
item.description: Broadcom's Enterprise Security Group advisory 39404, last revised on 2026-10-30, lists Carbon Black App Control Server, Symantec Endpoint Protection Manager (SEPM), the CloudSOC SpanVA Appliance and, since 2026-10-30, Content Analysis and Malware Analysis (CASMA) as affected by the PHP flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and gives no versions, fixes or workarounds. Broadcom's article 459982 names App Control Server 8.12.2 and 8.13.2 as the fixes for all supported versions; the SEPM builds 14.3.27716.10000 and 14.4.494.0000 rest on a community report that NCSC-NL's tracker accepts, because Broadcom's SEPM advisory needs a login. CISA lists both PHP flaws as exploited, and Broadcom's advisory says nothing about attacks on these products.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-109618 +1exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, Broadcom Symantec Endpoint Protection Manager, Carbon Black App Control Server, CloudSOC SpanVA and Content Analysis and Malware Analysis: PHP2Shell reaches the endpoint-security management servers; App Control Server 8.12.2 and 8.13.2 are the fixes Broadcom names

Broadcom's Enterprise Security Group advisory 39404, published on 2026-10-21 and last revised on 2026-10-30, lists four products as affected by the PHP flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: Carbon Black App Control Server (moved to affected on 2026-10-22), Symantec Endpoint Protection Manager (SEPM, 2026-10-22), the CloudSOC SpanVA Appliance (2026-10-23) and Content Analysis and Malware Analysis (CASMA), which moved from under investigation to affected on 2026-10-30; the page states no versions, fixes or workarounds, and lists Content Analysis (CAS), the Symantec Endpoint Protection agent, Symantec Endpoint Security, Data Loss Prevention, Cloud Secure Web Gateway and Zero Trust Network Access among the products that are not vulnerable (Broadcom, 2026-10-30). CISA added both PHP flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-26 (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-26); Broadcom's advisory says nothing about attacks on these products.

Broadcom's article 459982 says the App Control Server is affected in all supported versions and that builds 8.12.2 and 8.13.2 are available and contain only PHP-related changes: an installation on 8.12 or earlier may take either, one already on 8.13 must take 8.13.2 (Broadcom, 2026-10-22). For SEPM, NCSC-NL's tracker lists builds 14.3.27716.10000 and 14.4.494.0000 as the fixes, on the strength of a community report that cites Broadcom's SEPM advisory, which needs a login and which the maintainer did not verify (NCSC-NL, 2026-10-30). No fix is stated for the CloudSOC SpanVA Appliance or CASMA.

Exposure
A Symantec Endpoint Protection Manager, Carbon Black App Control Server, CloudSOC SpanVA appliance or CASMA whose management console or web service a hostile network can reach; Broadcom gives no version ranges, so every instance not on a fixed build counts. The flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are in the PHP runtime.
Detection
Broadcom publishes no indicator. For a server that was reachable before its fix, review shells and downloads started by the console's web service and outbound connections the server initiates; this is an inference, since the pages do not describe how these products run PHP.
Defender takeaway
Put these consoles on administrator networks now and on fixed builds as soon as they exist: App Control Server has its fix, SEPM's rests on an unverified reading, and CloudSOC SpanVA and CASMA have none. Re-read Broadcom's advisory 39404 before relying on a status, because CASMA changed on 2026-10-30.

item.title: Linux TCP use-after-free: Anthropic built a remote root exploit; Ubuntu and RHEL kernels still unfixed
item.description: The Linux kernel CVE team published CVE-2026-98432 on 2026-10-15, a use-after-free in the IPv4 TCP connection setup path that dates to Linux 4.4 and is reached by a SYN packet carrying IP options; the CNA scores it CVSS 9.8. Anthropic reports that Claude wrote an exploit giving a remote, unauthenticated attacker root command execution on servers with a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener, and the Go team says the bug is not specific to MPTCP and that Go programs enable MPTCP on Linux listeners by default. Debian's security kernels are fixed while Ubuntu 22.04 to 26.10 and RHEL 8 to 10 had no fixed kernel on 2026-10-30; no source reports public exploit code or attacks.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-98432NATOB2

CVE-2026-98432, Linux kernel IPv4 TCP: a use-after-free in connection setup, present since 4.4, has an Anthropic-built remote root exploit against MPTCP listeners; Debian is fixed, Ubuntu and Red Hat kernels are not yet (CVSS 9.8)

The Linux kernel CVE team published CVE-2026-98432 on 2026-10-15: a use-after-free in the IPv4 TCP connection setup path, introduced in Linux 4.4 and fixed upstream in 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 and 7.3-rc7 (Linux kernel CVE team, 2026-10-15). An unauthenticated peer starts it by sending TCP SYN packets that carry IPv4 options, and a retransmitted SYN or the ACK of the syncookie path can then touch the freed option memory (CIQ, 2026-10-30). Anthropic wrote on 2026-10-27 that Claude produced an exploit that lets a remote attacker send packets to a Linux server with a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener and run arbitrary commands as root without credentials (Anthropic, 2026-10-27). The Go team says the bug is not specific to MPTCP, that systems with no MPTCP listener may be open to similar attacks, and that since Go 1.24 Go programs enable MPTCP on Linux listen sockets by default (Go team, 2026-10-29). NCSC-NL judges large-scale abuse unlikely given the exploit's complexity and the mitigations distributions carry (translated from Dutch) (NCSC-NL, 2026-10-30), and BleepingComputer found no confirmed report of exploitation in the wild (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-30).

Severity is disputed: the CNA scores it 9.8, upstream 8.1 with high attack complexity (CIQ, 2026-10-30), and Red Hat rates it Critical for RHEL because it lets an unauthenticated remote attacker cause kernel memory corruption or an immediate crash over ordinary IPv4 TCP traffic, while saying reliable code execution needs precise heap control (Red Hat, 2026-10-31). Patch state as read on 2026-10-30 and 2026-10-31: Debian's security kernels 6.1.190-1 (bookworm) and 6.12.113-1 (trixie) are fixed (Debian Security Tracker, 2026-10-31); Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04, 26.04 and 26.10 are marked vulnerable with work in progress and 20.04, 18.04 and 16.04 vulnerable (Canonical, 2026-10-30); Red Hat lists RHEL 8, 9 and 10 as affected and RHEL 7 as not affected (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-30); BleepingComputer reports fixes for some kernel versions from Oracle Linux, Amazon Linux and SUSE (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-30); and CIQ had published no patched kernel for its RLC Pro LTS 9.6, RLC Pro LTS 8.10 or RLC Pro 10 variants and refers Rocky Linux community releases to Rocky errata (CIQ, 2026-10-30).

Exposure
A Linux host on a kernel below the fixed builds that accepts IPv4 TCP connections from an attacker; the demonstrated exploit needs an MPTCP listener, which sysctl net.mptcp.enabled shows as possible when it returns 1 and which matters for software built with Go 1.24 or newer, but CIQ's testing found that setting it to 0 leaves the plain-TCP path reachable (CIQ, 2026-10-30).
Detection
No source publishes an indicator. Because the trigger is a SYN packet with IP options (CIQ, 2026-10-30) and a lost race only fails the handshake, so the attacker can retry (Anthropic, 2026-10-27), repeated option-bearing SYNs from one source toward a listener in firewall or flow telemetry are the pattern the mechanism implies (an inference, since no source describes the traffic).
Defender takeaway
Install the distribution kernel and reboot as soon as it ships; Debian's is out, Ubuntu's and Red Hat's were not on 2026-10-30. Until then, CIQ's interim measure is a packet filter that drops IPv4 TCP packets whose header carries IP options before the TCP stack sees them, to be tested on one non-production host first because it also drops legitimate TCP traffic that carries IP options; disabling MPTCP alone does not remove the path (CIQ, 2026-10-30).

item.title: Drupal Commerce Core access bypass is exploited in the wild; update to 3.3.13 or 8.x-2.41 and audit orders
item.description: Drupal's advisory SA-CONTRIB-2026-254 of 2026-10-28 says an access bypass in the Commerce Core module, which adds a shopping cart and checkout to Drupal sites, is being actively exploited in the wild; the Drupal security team scores it 21 of 25, needing no authentication and affecting every module configuration. Commerce Core 3.0.0 up to but not including 3.3.13, and earlier releases before 8.x-2.41, are affected, and Drupal tells operators to update and audit their orders for inconsistencies. NCSC Switzerland issued its own advisory on 2026-10-30; Drupal says nothing on the method, the actor or the number of sites hit.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-118539exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-118539, Drupal Commerce Core: an access bypass in routes and entity fields is exploited against online stores, fixed in 3.3.13 and 8.x-2.41 (Drupal risk 21 of 25)

Drupal's advisory SA-CONTRIB-2026-254 of 2026-10-28 says Commerce Core "doesn't sufficiently protect certain routes and entity fields, leading to an access bypass that may financially impact the vendor" and that the flaw is being actively exploited in the wild (Drupal Security Team, 2026-10-28); The Hacker News carries the same wording (The Hacker News, 2026-10-30). The Drupal security team scores it 21 of 25, which SecurityWeek reads as exploitable without authentication whatever the module's configuration, and Drupal's statistics put the module on more than 42,000 sites (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-30). The affected releases are Commerce Core 3.0.0 up to but not including 3.3.13 and earlier releases before 8.x-2.41 (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-30). Drupal has not said how the bug is exploited, by whom, how many sites were targeted or whether it was exploited before the fix (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-30); NCSC Switzerland's advisory of 2026-10-30 describes the impact as unauthenticated manipulation of order-related data with financial loss for the shop operator (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-30).

Exposure
Any Drupal site running Commerce Core below 3.3.13 on 3.x or below 8.x-2.41 on earlier releases, including shops built on the module's decoupled APIs rather than its own cart and checkout (The Hacker News, 2026-10-30); a public body that sells goods, permits or fees through such a site is in scope. The same day's batch holds 38 further Drupal advisories for 21 contributed projects, nearly a dozen rated critical, among them code execution, account takeover and Commerce orders marked as paid through Stripe without payment (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-30).
Detection
Drupal's own guidance is an order audit for inconsistencies (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-30); checking each order's state, totals and payment status against the payment provider's records is the obvious test, an inference since no source names a method. The sources name no routes, parameters or request patterns; the web-server access log of the shop's API and checkout routes is the other record to review, an inference since nothing describes the requests.
Defender takeaway
Update Commerce Core to 3.3.13 or 8.x-2.41 now and audit orders; the flaw needs no login and the upgrade is the only mitigation the sources name. Check the other contributed modules the site runs against the advisories of 2026-10-28.

item.title: Update: PHP2Shell: Trend Micro Apex Central and Apex One await patches to 11 Nov; Quest KACE and NetApp ONTAP have fixes

item.content:encoded:
Update31 Oct 2026 03:40 UTCrun 2026-10-31T0256Z-intelsummaryaffected_productscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbodyentities

Trend Micro's PHP2Shell advisory, updated 2026-10-30, now lists critical patches for Deep Discovery Inspector and Email Inspector and adds Mobile Security for Enterprise as impacted with a patch due on 2026-11-17; the Apex Central and Apex One server patches stay due on 2026-11-11. item.title: privatim cloud guidance v3.02: public bodies keep their own keys for sensitive data; big-vendor SaaS mostly out
item.description: privatim, the conference of the Swiss data-protection authorities, revised its guidance on cloud-specific risks for public bodies on 2026-10-02 (version 3.02, replacing the version of 3 February 2022). For particularly sensitive personal data the public body must encrypt with keys only it can use, outsourcing such data or data under a statutory duty of confidentiality to standard SaaS from large international providers is in most cases inadmissible, and the body's top management is to confirm the residual risk in writing.
item.content:encoded:
ROUTINENATOA2

privatim revises its cloud guidance for Swiss public bodies (Merkblatt v3.02, 2 October 2026): sensitive data stays under the body's own keys, standard SaaS from Microsoft, Google, AWS and SAP is in most cases inadmissible for secrecy-bound data, and top management signs the residual risk

privatim, the conference of the Swiss data-protection authorities, dates version 3.02 of its guidance "Cloud-specific risks and measures" to 2 October 2026 (privatim, 2026-10-02); it replaces the version of 3 February 2022 (DCOD, 2026-10-27). For particularly sensitive personal data the public body must encrypt, the keys may be available only to it, and outsourcing such data, or data under a statutory duty of confidentiality, to SaaS from large international providers, with Microsoft, Google, AWS and SAP named, is in most cases inadmissible because of the untenable risk (privatim, 2026-10-02). Keys may stay with the provider only where no untenable risk follows and the provider is bound by contract to use them only with the body's express consent and to log every access (privatim, 2026-10-02).

The body, or its top management, is to confirm in writing that it has understood the risks and accepts the residual risk, and data the cloud services generate about their users, such as telemetry and logging data, is to be treated with the same care and contract terms as the content data (privatim, 2026-10-02). The five risk areas are contract design, places of processing including foreign authority access, confidentiality with encryption and key management, user data, and sub-processors (privatim, 2026-10-02).

Defender takeaway
The guidance addresses public bodies subject to Swiss data-protection law; a body that runs or plans standard SaaS from the named providers for sensitive or secrecy-bound data is advised to keep its own encryption keys, to have top management sign the residual risk, and to hold provider telemetry and logs about its users to the same contract terms.

item.title: Lumen: Volt Typhoon's Silent Train relay chains fronted zero-days against SD-WAN, N-central and KACE
item.description: Lumen's Black Lotus Labs reports that Volt Typhoon ran exploitation, credential access and exfiltration through Silent Train, rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT and enterprise devices that it rebuilt for each operation, and that its monitoring uncovered one likely and four confirmed zero-day campaigns against endpoint and network management platforms and SD-WAN orchestrators, among them Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN, N-able N-central and Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator. The reported victims are US-centred and the report names no Swiss or European victim.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Silent Train: Lumen's Black Lotus Labs describes the rotating relay network Volt Typhoon used for one likely and four confirmed zero-day campaigns against management and control-plane platforms (Quest KACE, Versa Director, N-able N-central, Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN, Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator)

Lumen's Black Lotus Labs reports that Volt Typhoon used a covert framework it calls Silent Train, first seen in late 2023, for the phases that need protection: exploitation, credential access, data exfiltration and continued access to victims (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28). A session starts from a virtual private server outside the US, passes through compromised non-US SOHO and IoT devices and leaves through a compromised US device before the victim; more than 27 device classes were enrolled, from TP-Link routers and Netgear Orbi devices to Fortinet appliances and CyberPanel servers, and the enterprise platforms stayed in chains for one to three months as final hops (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28). The operators exploit exposed web interfaces on the relay devices and deploy only what chained SSH needs, namely temporary SSH services, keys, configuration files and living-off-the-land utilities, with reverse tunnels over open-source proxies in later variants; sessions averaged about four hours, and at the end the operators removed all artifacts and dismantled the chain (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28).

Lumen says its monitoring helped identify one likely and four confirmed zero-day campaigns against endpoint and network management platforms and SD-WAN orchestrators: Quest KACE, where the activity looked like an undisclosed flaw, affected more than 30 victims and fell after Quest's October 2025 updates (a moderate-confidence assessment); Versa Director in 2024; the N-able N-central flaws CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876; Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN through CVE-2026-20127, exploited by late 2025 and after Cisco's February 2026 disclosure; and Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator through the zero-day later designated CVE-2026-16812 (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28). Post-incident analysis found in-memory webshells, credential harvesting and abuse of native platform features such as endpoint control and remote file transfers, and in several cases erased or altered logs (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28). The victims it names are US government, telecommunications, defence-industrial, managed-service and critical-infrastructure organisations, concentrated in Hawaii, California and Texas, and it names no European or Swiss victim (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28). The Hacker News carries the same findings from a report Lumen shared with it (The Hacker News, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
Internet-reachable management and control-plane platforms (endpoint management, SD-WAN controllers and orchestrators, out-of-band administration), and edge devices with exposed web interfaces, which can be enrolled as relay hops without any data of the owner being the target.
Detection
Telemetry classes are administrative logins, API calls, remote file transfers and configuration changes on management platforms outside normal administration hours or workflow, in-memory web shells that leave no file on disk, and, on edge devices, temporary SSH services, unfamiliar keys and outbound reverse tunnels to unfamiliar upstream hosts (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28).
Defender takeaway
Restrict the administrative interfaces of management and control-plane platforms to a VPN, jump host or management network and prioritise their patching, as Lumen advises, and treat an edge device that shows temporary SSH services or reverse tunnels as a possible relay in someone else's intrusion chain.

item.title: CrowdStrike: VAPOR PANDA runs ARTEX against 200+ organisations, European foreign ministries among them
item.description: CrowdStrike reports that from 2026-10-17 the China-nexus actor VAPOR PANDA used the ARTEX agent framework, driven mainly by the DeepSeek model, against more than 200 organisations worldwide, with the controller CrowdStrike saw directing exploitation in at least 14 countries, including foreign ministries in Europe, a European country's presidency, prime minister's office and defence, justice, finance and intelligence entities, and a Greek government entity. CrowdStrike confirmed post-exploitation at nine organisations, with the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor loaded by a renamed legitimate binary, and says this campaign is separate from the Storm-0940 ARTEX activity Microsoft reported.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB3

VAPOR PANDA: CrowdStrike reports a China-nexus actor running the ARTEX agent framework against more than 200 organisations from 17 October, among them foreign ministries in Europe and a Greek government entity, and deploying the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor

CrowdStrike OverWatch reports that from 2026-10-17 a single ARTEX controller linked to VAPOR PANDA infrastructure directed exploitation against entities in at least 14 countries over 11 days, and that the campaign reached more than 200 organisations, including foreign ministries in Europe (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). One engagement focused on a single European country, its foreign ministry, presidency, prime minister's office and defence, justice, finance and intelligence entities, and another targeted 19 US organisations in pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, defence, nuclear and finance (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). CrowdStrike confirmed post-exploitation at nine organisations and password spraying and credential scanning against at least 12 more, among them government entities in Europe (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). CrowdStrike states that the campaign is separate from the Storm-0940 ARTEX activity Microsoft reported and is VAPOR PANDA's first observed use of AI-driven tooling (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29).

The framework ran mainly on the DeepSeek model, with a human operator steering the agents at decision points while they pursued web, cloud, container, Active Directory, mail and VPN paths in parallel (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). In transcripts at a US pharmaceutical company the agent chained an unsigned SAML assertion with an XML external entity flaw to query the cloud instance metadata service and obtain a role that could issue administration commands to thousands of instances; at a second it deployed web shells, abused an unauthenticated orchestration service for root in a container environment, read LAPS passwords and abused resource-based constrained delegation (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). Against a Greek government entity the operator supplied a 2022 directory export from the mail server whose authentication keys had likely not been rotated; the agent forged an administrator token, read mailboxes and used VPN configurations from a user's sent mail, with a VPN client key the operator described as coming from a May 2024 email leak, to reach the internal network (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). The operator also told the agents to find domain Windows hosts without the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). At a Middle East interior ministry and a Latin American foreign ministry the actor loaded the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor through a legitimate GameHook binary renamed svchost.exe that loads a malicious DLL (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). No Swiss target is named.

Exposure

Its ransomware cases (27 percent of engagements) show help-desk vishing that leads the victim to allow remote access through a legitimate remote-management tool, and operators who uninstall or terminate EDR, including with vulnerable drivers.
item.content:encoded:
ROUTINENATOB2

ANNUAL REPORT: Cisco Talos Incident Response trends Q3 2026: public administration tied with finance as the most targeted sector, help-desk vishing into remote-management tools, and ransomware operators uninstalling and killing EDR

Cisco Talos Incident Response reports that in Q3 2026 financial organisations made up 18 percent of its engagements, tying with public administration as the most targeted sector (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29). Phishing was the leading initial-access technique at 37 percent of engagements and exploitation of public-facing applications second at 33 percent; the phishing cases include numerous actors who phone the victim as the IT help desk to get remote access allowed through a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29). Ransomware and pre-ransomware cases were 27 percent of engagements, with The Gentlemen, Qilin, Rhysida and the closed group Interlock among the families and a new variant, VYPR, that Talos calls operationally immature: it had no leak site when seen, reused leaked Conti-derived source code and exfiltrated over several days (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29).

The VYPR intrusion began with a vishing call that had the user start a Microsoft Quick Assist session; the actor then used RMM software that ran PowerShell to download and install an MSI from a remote address, with MeshAgent, Rclone, PsExec, an IP scanner and mstsc as tools, and disabled EDR with several vulnerable drivers (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29). Interlock operators repeatedly tried to uninstall Cisco Secure Endpoint, used PsExec and taskkill to end security services and integrity checkers, turned off Windows Defender real-time protection and cleared event logs (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29). Talos names insufficient logging (over 40 percent of engagements), weak credential and secret handling, and absent or incomplete MFA as the most common weaknesses, and recommends centralised logging with at least 90 days of retention (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29).

Exposure
An organisation whose help desk or staff can be reached by phone and whose endpoints permit Quick Assist or an unapproved RMM agent; Talos names public administration among the most targeted sectors in its caseload.
Detection
In process-creation and software-install telemetry, an RMM or Quick Assist session started after an inbound call, followed by PowerShell run under the RMM agent that downloads an installer from an external address; in endpoint and service-control telemetry, attempts to uninstall the EDR agent, PsExec or taskkill ending security services, Defender real-time protection switched off, vulnerable kernel drivers loaded, and event logs cleared.
Defender takeaway
Treat a remote-support session that nobody at the help desk started as the vishing signal and inventory which RMM tools and Quick Assist are permitted on endpoints; alert on EDR uninstall and security-service termination as a ransomware precursor; and centralise logs with the 90-day minimum retention Talos recommends, because actors delete logs on the endpoint.

item.title: WordPress 7.1.4 fixes an unauthenticated upgrade-window RCE race; Wordfence sees probing, so confirm the auto-update ran
item.description: WordPress 7.1.4 of 2026-10-28 fixes a weakness in the core upgrade process that lets an unauthenticated attacker reach the staged installer and run code on the server during a full-package core update, in versions 4.7 to 7.1.3, with backports for every branch down to 4.7. Wordfence reports more than 18,500 probing requests in the first 21 hours, while Patchstack calls the race hard to win and says it needs a web-reachable staging directory; no source gives a CVE identifier.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOA2

WordPress core 4.7 to 7.1.3: an unauthenticated race in the core update process can lead to remote code execution, fixed in 7.1.4 and backported to every supported branch, with Wordfence reporting exploitation attempts and no CVE assigned in the sources

WordPress 7.1.4, released on 2026-10-28, fixes a weakness in the upgrade process that can lead to remote code execution during the upgrade window, and backports follow for every branch that receives security fixes, currently through 4.7 (WordPress.org, 2026-10-28); WordPress's release documentation counts 22 vulnerabilities, as Wordfence reports (Wordfence, 2026-10-29). During a core update with a complete package, the new files are unpacked into a predictable directory under wp-content/upgrade; the temporary copy includes the installer, and an unauthenticated attacker who requests it at the right moment can interact with the staged copy and reach PHP code execution (Wordfence, 2026-10-29). Wordfence scores it CVSS 8.1 for versions 4.7 through 7.1.3 and states that the attack complexity is high, because the attacker needs web access to the staging tree and must win a race that lasted only seconds in its lab (Wordfence, 2026-10-29). Patchstack reads the same flaw as needing wp-content/upgrade/ to be reachable over the web, notes that the sink dates back to WordPress 2.8 and that the window returns on every update, unattended ones included, and would not call it practical to exploit (Patchstack, 2026-10-28).

Wordfence reports that its new firewall rule matched within nine minutes of deployment and that it recorded more than 18,500 requests for staged setup-config.php installer paths in the first 21 hours, with two large sources polling small groups of sites for about 14.5 hours, which it reads as attempts to catch the update window (Wordfence, 2026-10-29). No source reports a successful compromise, and no source assigns a CVE identifier. The fix randomises the staging directory, adds an index guard and prevents unsafe promotion of staged configuration data (Wordfence, 2026-10-29). Most sites receive the release through automatic background updates, which Wordfence says should be checked rather than assumed (Wordfence, 2026-10-29).

Exposure
Any WordPress site on 4.7 to 7.1.3 that runs a full-package core update, automatic ones included, with wp-content/upgrade/ reachable from the internet; Dashboard > Updates shows the running version, and the fixed releases are 7.1.4 and the backport of each branch (7.0.8, 6.9.11, 6.8.12, 6.7.11, 6.6.11 and the earlier branches listed by Wordfence down to 4.7.39) (Wordfence, 2026-10-29).
Detection
In web server access logs, requests under wp-content/upgrade/ and for setup-config.php inside a staging directory, repeated from one source against a few sites as Wordfence saw (Wordfence, 2026-10-29); between updates the directory holds only an index.php (Patchstack, 2026-10-28). Where an update ran while the site was unpatched and the directory was reachable, confirm that wp-config.php and the database it names are unchanged, because the fix exists to stop unsafe promotion of staged configuration data.

Triage: a request to a staging path outside an update window finds only an index.php and is probing, not compromise; a successful response from the staged installer during an update is the event that matters.

Defender takeaway
Confirm that the automatic update completed on every site instead of assuming it, and deny web access to wp-content/upgrade/ at the web server, because a firewall that WordPress itself loads cannot block the request: the staged copy loads from its own files (Patchstack, 2026-10-28); Wordfence's blocking rule helps only where its firewall is set up to run before direct PHP requests reach their file (Wordfence, 2026-10-29).

item.title: Cisco ASA and FTD SSL VPN reload flaw is exploited and on CISA KEV; fixes in every branch, no workaround
item.description: Cisco's advisory of 2026-10-28 fixes CVE-2026-76418, a logic error in the remote access SSL VPN of Secure Firewall ASA and Secure FTD that lets an unauthenticated attacker reload the device with a crafted connection request when a tunnel group uses secondary authentication, and says Cisco's PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in October 2026; CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-29. Cisco names no actor, offers no workaround and lists first fixed releases for every ASA and FTD branch.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHCVE-2026-76418exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-76418, Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and Secure FTD: a crafted request to the remote access SSL VPN reloads the device when a tunnel group uses secondary authentication; Cisco reports active exploitation and CISA lists it (CVSS 3.1 8.6)

Cisco's advisory of 2026-10-28 describes CVE-2026-76418, a logic error in the remote access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and Secure FTD: an unauthenticated, remote attacker who sends a crafted request while connecting to the SSL VPN makes the device reload, and a successful VPN login is not required to reach the affected processing path (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Cisco says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in October 2026 and names no actor or victim (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28); CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-29 (CISA, 2026-10-29), and CERT-FR restates the advisory (ANSSI / CERT-FR, 2026-10-29). The stated impact is a reload and denial of service, scored CVSS 3.1 8.6 with availability as the only impact; no code execution or data access is described (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).

The first fixed releases are ASA 9.16.4.104 (for 9.16 and earlier), 9.18.4.96, 9.20.4.50, 9.22.3.200, 9.23.1.48, 9.24.1.27 and 9.24.10.1, and FTD 7.0.11 (for 7.0 and earlier), 7.2.13, 7.4.9, 7.6.7, 7.7.14, 10.0.3 and 10.1.1 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Cisco lists no workaround; its mitigation is to remove secondary authentication from the tunnel group, which lowers the security posture of the remote access VPN, or, where DefaultWEBVPNGroup does not use secondary authentication, to disable the tunnel group list with no tunnel-group-list enable (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Cisco confirms that Secure FMC, Cloud-delivered Firewall, cdFMC and Secure Access are not affected (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
An ASA or FTD unit below the first fixed release of its branch whose running configuration has webvpn enabled on an interface and secondary-authentication-server-group on any tunnel group; the default tunnel group DefaultWEBVPNGroup counts even when the tunnel group list is disabled. On FTD, read the deployed remote access VPN policy and the resulting configuration in FMC or FDM (Devices > VPN > Remote Access) (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).
Detection
Neither Cisco nor CISA publishes an indicator. The mechanism points at device availability telemetry: unexpected reloads, HA failover flaps, uptime resets and crash files on units that terminate the remote access VPN, read against VPN authentication logs for connection attempts from external addresses that never complete a login.

Triage: a reload also follows upgrades, HA events and hardware faults; a reload that coincides with unauthenticated SSL VPN connection attempts from an external address is the pattern the stated mechanism produces.

Defender takeaway
Upgrade the units that terminate remote access SSL VPN with secondary authentication this week, perimeter units first; Cisco states denial of service as the only impact, so patching leaves no further step, and removing secondary authentication as a stop-gap trades an outage risk for a weaker VPN login.

CISA added CVE-2026-46300 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-28 and says it can be chained with the PHP2Shell flaws to implant PHP webshells and run commands as root; Dream Research describes such a chain used against 24 firewalls of one unnamed vendor and a US government-affiliated network. The CVE record moves to exploited, the priority from notable to high, and the earlier statement that no source reports exploitation of this CVE is replaced. Removed from the text: the sentence that an attacker can modify any file the user can read (the Detection line still carries it) and, from the summary, the clause on Aikido's report of working Kubernetes exploits for the Dirty Frag family.

CISA added CVE-2026-46300 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-28 and says in the entry that the flaw can be chained with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to implant PHP webshells and run commands as root, naming no actor or victim (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28). Dream Research describes a chain of this kind from artifacts its tooling recovered: a custom, non-public PHP2Shell build, tailored to the management web server of one large vendor's firewall software that runs PHP 8.0.30, gives code execution as the nobody user, and the Fragnesia exploit then overwrites /etc/pam.d/su in the page cache so that su root succeeds without a password; Dream says SELinux confines the web server's domain from modifying system files and that the whole chain runs in one HTTP request in under 15 minutes (Dream Research, 2026-10-27). From about 19,000 internet-facing firewalls of that vendor that it found through a search engine, the attacker narrowed to 240 in the United States, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea, rooted 24 and planted a PHP webshell on each; on the second of two firewalls of a US government-affiliated organization (the first crashed) it set up an outbound SSH tunnel kept up by a systemd service and an rc.local entry, rooted the organization's firewall management server through the tunnel, decrypted the LDAP service-account password with root access and sprayed passwords against a domain that had no lockout threshold (Dream Research, 2026-10-27). Dream could not tell whether any of the Active Directory attacks succeeded, does not name the vendor, calls the campaign apparently Chinese and AI-assisted and does not attribute it to a named actor (Dream Research, 2026-10-27).

Open finding: CVE-2026-46300, Linux kernel: local privilege escalation via xfrm ESP-in-TCP ("Fragnesia"), listed by CISA as exploited and chained with the PHP2Shell flaws to reach root, PoC public →

item.title: PHP2Shell: Trend Micro Apex Central and Apex One await patches to 11 Nov; Quest KACE and NetApp ONTAP have fixes
item.description: Trend Micro's advisory, last updated 2026-10-30, lists Apex Central and the on-premises Apex One server as impacted by the PHP flaws with critical patches due on 2026-11-11 and interim mitigations, shows critical patches for Deep Discovery Inspector and Email Inspector, and adds Mobile Security for Enterprise as impacted with a patch due on 2026-11-17; Quest says all KACE SMA and SDA versions are affected, with SMA 15.0 CU5 and 15.1 CU2 and the SDA 9.3 hotfix out and advice to block ports 80, 443 and 52230 until applied; and NetApp's advisory lists ONTAP 9 as affected only by CVE-2026-109618, with attacker access as the www user restricted to the PHP jail and hotfix builds from 9.14.1P18HF1 to 9.19.1P4. None of the three vendors reports an exploited case in what was read, although CISA lists both flaws as exploited.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-109618 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, PHP2Shell in management servers and storage: Trend Micro Apex Central and Apex One server have no fix until 2026-11-11, Quest KACE SMA and SDA have fixes and should block ports 80, 443 and 52230 until patched, and NetApp ONTAP 9 is affected by CVE-2026-109618 only, inside the PHP jail

Trend Micro's customer advisory KA-0024802, last updated on 2026-10-30, lists Apex Central and the Apex One on-premises server as impacted by CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 with a critical patch expected on 2026-11-11 and an interim mitigation page for each; Mobile Security for Enterprise is impacted with a patch due on 2026-11-17, Trend Micro Web Security in the cloud is due on 2026-11-06 and Deep Discovery Analyzer on 2026-11-12, Apex One as a Service was addressed on 2026-10-23, and the table lists critical patches for Deep Discovery Inspector and Email Inspector (Trend Micro, 2026-10-30). Trend Micro says it has not seen successful exploitation in its products or services and asks customers to restrict the impacted management servers and consoles to trusted addresses until the patches ship (Trend Micro, 2026-10-30).

Quest's knowledge-base article says all versions of the KACE Systems Management Appliance (SMA) and Systems Deployment Appliance (SDA) are affected and that CVE-2026-115560 does not affect them; KACE SMA 15.0 CU5 (15.0.378) and 15.1 CU2 (15.1.177) with PHP 8.4.27 were published on 2026-10-23, the cumulative updates 15.0 Patch 4 and 15.1 Patch 1 do not contain the fix, and the SDA 9.3 hotfix 9.3.312 with PHP 8.3.36 followed (Quest Software, 2026-10-28); hotfix 9.3.313 of 2026-10-29 also covers systems on hotfix versions 9.3.305-9.3.111 and on GA version 9.3.304 (Quest Software, 2026-10-29). Until an appliance is updated Quest says to block all public internet access and, because a potentially exploitable communication path remains after the agent tunnel on port 52230 is established, to block inbound web traffic including ports 80, 443 and 52230 (Quest Software, 2026-10-28).

NetApp's advisory lists ONTAP 9 as affected only by CVE-2026-109618, scored CVSS 4.0 9.2, where an unauthenticated attacker could potentially gain access as the www user but would be restricted to the PHP jail, and lists the hotfix builds 9.14.1P18HF1, 9.15.1P20HF1, 9.16.1P16HF1, 9.17.1P11HF1, 9.18.1P8HF1, 9.19.1P3HF1 and, since revision 10.0 of 2026-10-29, 9.19.1P4 (NetApp, 2026-10-26; NetApp, 2026-10-29). NetApp's knowledge-base article names all ONTAP web services as affected, System Manager, the SPI web portal, the REST API, ZAPI and HTTP and HTTPS access, and recommends upgrading to a fixed version and undoing any workaround afterwards (NetApp Knowledge Base, 2026-10-26). CISA lists both PHP flaws as exploited since 2026-10-26, although none of the three vendors reports an exploited case (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A Trend Micro Apex Central, Apex One or Mobile Security for Enterprise server whose console or web endpoints a hostile network can reach; any KACE SMA or SDA, whose web ports and agent port 52230 are named; any ONTAP 9 cluster whose web services are reachable and that runs a release other than the fixed builds (Trend Micro, 2026-10-28; Quest Software, 2026-10-28; NetApp Knowledge Base, 2026-10-26).
Detection
None of the three vendors publishes an indicator. For a management server or appliance that was reachable before its fix, the telemetry to review is shells and downloads started by its web service and outbound connections the server initiates; this is an inference, since the pages do not describe the attack.
Defender takeaway
Take the Trend Micro, KACE and ONTAP management interfaces off untrusted networks first and patch as the fixes ship; Trend Micro says its status table is updated as its inventory continues, so re-read it before relying on a date (Trend Micro, 2026-10-30).

item.title: F5 BIG-IP is affected by PHP2Shell: fixes are in 17.1.3.7, 17.5.1.11 and 21.1.0.4; APM data plane and TMUI exposed
item.description: F5's release notes for BIG-IP 17.1.3.7, 17.5.1.11 and 21.1.0.4, each updated on 2026-10-24, list K000163821 as the fix for the PHP flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and call each a critical release whose only new changes are PHP fixes. NCSC-NL's record of K000163821 puts BIG-IP 17.1.0 to 17.1.3, 17.5.0 to 17.5.1 and 21.1.0 in scope, through the Configuration utility of all modules and through the access-profile data plane of APM and SSL Orchestrator; F5's article itself could not be read, and nothing found reports an attack on BIG-IP, although CISA lists both flaws as exploited.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-109618 +1exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, F5 BIG-IP: the PHP2Shell flaws reach the Configuration utility of every module and the APM and SSL Orchestrator access profiles on 17.1.0 to 17.1.3, 17.5.0 to 17.5.1 and 21.1.0, and F5's cumulative critical releases 17.1.3.7, 17.5.1.11 and 21.1.0.4 carry the fix

F5's release notes for BIG-IP 17.1.3.7, 21.1.0.4 and 17.5.1.11, each updated on 2026-10-24, list K000163821 as the reference for the fix of the PHP vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and describe each build as a critical release whose only new changes are PHP vulnerability fixes and which is cumulative and includes earlier hardened and critical releases (F5, 2026-10-24; F5, 2026-10-24; F5, 2026-10-24). NCSC-NL records F5 as confirming that BIG-IP 17.1.0 to 17.1.3, 17.5.0 to 17.5.1 and 21.1.0 are vulnerable through the Configuration utility control plane in all modules and, for APM and SSL Orchestrator, through the access-profile data plane, and that earlier affected releases stay vulnerable until updated (NCSC-NL, 2026-10-26). CISA lists both PHP flaws as exploited since 2026-10-26; nothing found reports an attack on BIG-IP (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A BIG-IP on 17.1.0 to 17.1.3, 17.5.0 to 17.5.1 or 21.1.0 whose Configuration utility is reachable from a network the attacker can reach, or that publishes an APM or SSL Orchestrator access profile (NCSC-NL, 2026-10-26).
Detection
F5's article on exploitation and mitigations could not be read and no indicator is published in the sources found. The telemetry to review on an exposed system is access to the Configuration utility and the access-profile web paths from untrusted sources, and shells or downloads started by the web service; this is an inference, not an F5 statement.
Defender takeaway
Move to the cumulative critical release of your train and read K000163821 in a browser for F5's own mitigation list; until then keep the Configuration utility off untrusted networks, and treat an APM or SSL Orchestrator system that was exposed and unpatched as needing a compromise check.

item.title: Check Point: PHP2Shell hits gateway VPN and portal web interfaces; hotfixes out, R81.20 package reissued 28 October
item.description: Check Point's advisory sk1000302, last modified 2026-10-29, says the PHP flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS 9.2 each) can give remote code execution through the web interfaces of Force, Spark and Cloud firewalls that use Mobile Access, SSL Network Extender VPN, SAML-realm VPN authentication, the Identity Awareness captive portal, the UserCheck portal or Zero Phishing. Hotfixes exist for R81.20, R82, R82.10 and R82.20 and for Spark R82.00 and R81.10; the R81.20 package was reissued on 2026-10-28 for gateways that use Mobile Access, and a hotfix for the end-of-support gateway release R81.10 followed on 2026-10-29. The sk makes no statement on exploitation of Check Point products, and CISA lists both flaws as exploited.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-109618 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, Check Point Force, Spark and Cloud firewalls: the PHP2Shell flaws reach the web interfaces of gateways that run Mobile Access, SSL Network Extender, SAML-realm VPN, the Identity Awareness captive portal, UserCheck or Zero Phishing; hotfixes since 2026-10-23, the R81.20 package reissued on 2026-10-28 (CVSS 9.2)

Check Point's advisory sk1000302, created on 2026-10-21 and last modified on 2026-10-29, says that under certain circumstances the PHP flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both scored CVSS 9.2, may allow remote code execution through firewall web interfaces (Check Point, 2026-10-29). Affected are Force, Spark and Cloud firewalls that use one or more of Mobile Access Portal (not Spark), Remote Access VPN with SSL Network Extender (not Spark), Remote Access VPN with SAML realm authentication, the Identity Awareness captive portal, the UserCheck portal and Zero Phishing, on R81.20, R82, R82.10 and R82.20 and on Spark R81.10.x and R82.00.x; R80 to R81.10 and the older Spark lines are end of support and also listed (Check Point, 2026-10-29). Check Point's portal and SaaS services are already patched, Security Management and Log Servers are not affected, and its products are not vulnerable to the third PHP issue, CVE-2026-115560 (Check Point, 2026-10-29).

The hotfix, first published on 2026-10-23, implements the PHP 7.4 fix, is compatible with every Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator take, goes on each gateway, cluster member, security-group member or standalone server and needs a reboot; the R82, R82.10 and R82.20 packages were reissued on 2026-10-26 to support standalone deployments, and the R81.20 package was reissued on 2026-10-28 to fix a Mobile Access problem, must sit on take 166 or higher and is required where the Mobile Access Portal is used (Check Point, 2026-10-29). For the gateway packages the fix is also planned for the Jumbo Hotfix Accumulators of 2026-11-11, and Spark has R82.00.11 (build 998002823) and R81.10.17 (build 996004992) (Check Point, 2026-10-29); a hotfix for the end-of-support R81.10 gateway release was published on 2026-10-29 at 11:30 GMT (Check Point, 2026-10-29). Until a hotfix is installed, Check Point's mitigation is a block in cp-httpd.conf that denies requests with a multipart Content-Type, followed by a restart of the portals, which is removed before installing the hotfix; R82.20 gateways are also protected by the "PHP Remote Code Execution" IPS signature even when IPS is not enabled (Check Point, 2026-10-29). CISA lists both PHP flaws as exploited since 2026-10-26, and the sk makes no statement on exploitation of Check Point gateways (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A gateway on a listed release with at least one of the six portal or VPN features in use; a gateway with none of them is outside the scope Check Point states (Check Point, 2026-10-29).
Detection
Check Point publishes no indicator and no post-compromise check. The web daemon's access logs for the portal paths, shells or downloads started by the gateway's web process, and outbound connections that the gateway itself initiates are the telemetry to review on a gateway that faced the internet before the fix; this is an inference, since the sk does not describe the attack.
Defender takeaway
Install the hotfix on every gateway that publishes a portal or VPN; where it has to wait, apply the cp-httpd.conf mitigation, and treat a gateway that was exposed and unpatched as needing a compromise check, because Check Point's page does not say whether patching removes a foothold.

item.title: SafeDep and JFrog: the testmetest npm worm now runs on import, so --ignore-scripts does not stop it; 42 repos armed
item.description: SafeDep and JFrog describe an npm worm, tracked as testmetest, whose newest builds start when an application imports the package, so installing with --ignore-scripts does not stop it. It steals SSH, registry, cloud, CI and AI-tool credentials, publishes new patch versions of the victim's own packages, and wipes the home directory when the stolen GitHub token is revoked. SafeDep counts 19 packages from one operator between 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-27; JFrog found 42 armed GitHub repositories of 11 legitimate owners; neither lab names an actor.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

testmetest: an npm worm in the Miasma and Shai-Hulud family now starts when an application imports the package, so install with --ignore-scripts no longer protects, and JFrog finds 42 third-party GitHub repositories already armed with its publisher

SafeDep counts 19 npm packages from the same operator between 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-27, eight of them published through four npm accounts, that carry a worm sharing code with the June Miasma worm and adding the token-revocation wiper of Mini Shai-Hulud; SafeDep has not confirmed the lineage, and JFrog says its evidence does not establish that the original Miasma operators are responsible (SafeDep, 2026-10-27; JFrog Security Research, 2026-10-26). The install trigger has changed twice: first a command expansion in a binding.gyp file, with no install script; then a postinstall script that loads a native addon which decodes and starts the worm; and, since SafeDep's update of 27 October, an addon that runs when an application imports the package, so a hardening step that disables install scripts does not stop it (SafeDep, 2026-10-27).

The payload exits on CIS locales and in known analysis sandboxes. It steals SSH keys, registry and Git credentials, .env files, browser logins, AI-tool, cloud, Vault and Kubernetes secrets and GitHub Actions secrets read from runner memory (SafeDep, 2026-10-27). It exfiltrates by committing encrypted data, with the victim's encrypted GitHub token, to a new public repository in the victim's own account, injects a GitLab CI job that requests npm and PyPI OIDC tokens, adds its loader to the victim's npm packages and publishes new patch versions, republishes to PyPI and RubyGems, commits a fake CodeQL workflow and AI-agent configuration files that infect the host again, and copies itself over SSH to the hosts in known_hosts (SafeDep, 2026-10-27). A persistence service checks the stolen GitHub token every 45 seconds for 48 hours and on an authentication failure deletes the home directory (SafeDep, 2026-10-27). JFrog found 42 armed third-party GitHub repositories of 11 legitimate owners with hooks for AI coding assistants and IDEs, and says the payload blobs were large enough to evade GitHub's search and API paths (JFrog Security Research, 2026-10-26).

Exposure
Any developer endpoint, build agent or CI runner that installed or imported one of the operator's packages, and any GitHub or GitLab account whose token such a host held (SafeDep, 2026-10-27).
Detection
In package metadata, a binding.gyp whose sources field runs node in a package with no C or C++ sources, a postinstall that requires a .node file and discards errors beside a large high-entropy file, and prebuilt addons with no native source; on endpoints and CI runners, a node process that downloads or finds and runs the Bun runtime and a child node process started from a temporary path named after its process ID; in GitHub and GitLab audit logs, a new public repository in a developer's own account with a generic project description, commits with a fixed automated-sync message, commits that add AI-assistant configuration files (.claude, .cursor, .gemini, .vscode tasks, CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md), an injected CI job that requests OIDC tokens, and unexpected patch releases of your own packages (SafeDep, 2026-10-27).
Defender takeaway
An install that ran with scripts disabled is not clean once the package has been imported; for an affected host SafeDep's order is to disconnect it, remove persistence first, rotate all credentials, check the accounts for the repositories and commits above and reinstall the operating system (SafeDep, 2026-10-27). Because the wiper is triggered by the token's revocation, the host is isolated and cleaned before the GitHub token is revoked.

item.title: ESET: an emailed RAR ran code on MDaemon servers via ClamAV's UnRAR; fixed in MDaemon 26.0.4, ClamAV 1.4.6 and 1.5.4
item.description: ESET reports an active campaign in Ukraine in which Russia-aligned attackers exploited MDaemon mail servers: a crafted RAR archive mailed to any address makes MDaemon invoke ClamAV, whose old bundled UnRAR library carries the path-traversal flaw CVE-2025-8088, and the exploit writes a malicious DLL to the server with no user interaction. MDaemon fixed it in 26.0.4 on 2026-08-25, and ClamAV's own notes show that every Windows ClamAV from 0.101.0 to 1.5.3 is affected, fixed in 1.4.6 and 1.5.4. The attackers deployed the HELLAGE mail-stealing backdoor and the Telegram-controlled HELLTAG backdoor.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2025-8088exploitedNATOB2

MDaemon mail server below 26.0.4 and Windows ClamAV 0.101.0 to 1.5.3: a crafted RAR emailed to any address runs code on the server through the bundled UnRAR flaw CVE-2025-8088, and ESET saw Russia-aligned attackers use it in Ukraine to deploy the HELLAGE and HELLTAG backdoors

ESET reports an active campaign in Ukraine in which Russia-aligned attackers exploited MDaemon mail servers and deployed two backdoor families, HELLAGE and HELLTAG (ESET Research, 2026-10-28). MDaemon uses ClamAV to scan attachments of incoming mail; old ClamAV versions carry CVE-2025-8088, the WinRAR path-traversal flaw ESET uncovered last year, which ESET says was fixed in ClamAV's source on 27 July 2025 (the release notes below date the fixed ClamAV builds 2026-08-07), while MDaemon kept shipping an old libclamunrar.dll until MDaemon 26.0.4 of 2026-08-25 (ESET Research, 2026-10-28). The chain ESET describes: a crafted RAR archive is mailed to any address at a vulnerable server, MDaemon invokes ClamAV to scan it, and the exploit writes a malicious DLL to the server's file system with no user interaction, so the message carries no lure (ESET Research, 2026-10-28). CERT-UA names the backdoors: HELLAGE steals email messages and other data, talks to a hardcoded server and can deploy more malware, and HELLTAG takes commands, transfers files and does reconnaissance through a hardcoded Telegram bot; ESET cannot attribute the campaign to a known Russia-aligned actor (ESET Research, 2026-10-28).

The exposure is wider than MDaemon. ClamAV's release notes of 2026-08-07 say it adopted the upstream UnRAR fix for CVE-2025-8088, which rejects path separators in NTFS alternate data stream names so that extraction cannot leave ClamAV's temporary scan directory on Windows, and that the issue affects ClamAV 0.101.0 through 1.5.3 with the fix in 1.4.6 and 1.5.4 (ClamAV, 2026-08-07). CISA has listed CVE-2025-8088 in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog since 2025-08-12 (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
An MDaemon server on Windows below 26.0.4 that accepts inbound mail (ESET Research, 2026-10-28), and any other Windows host that scans mail or files with ClamAV 0.101.0 to 1.5.3 (ClamAV, 2026-08-07).
Detection
Because the attack needs no lure, the mail log shows an ordinary message with a RAR attachment. The telemetry that matters is file creation of a DLL by the ClamAV or mail-service scanning process outside ClamAV's temporary scan directory, inbound RAR attachments whose member names carry alternate-data-stream syntax with path separators, and the mail service process starting unexpected children or connecting to Telegram's bot interface; these follow from the described chain and are not an ESET detection list. An update does not remove a DLL or backdoor that was already written, so check the server after patching.
Defender takeaway
Patch the mail scanning path first on any internet-facing Windows mail server, then look for unexpected DLLs and persistence and treat stored mail as exposed, since HELLAGE steals email (ESET Research, 2026-10-28).

item.title: Huntress: phished MDM enrolments push ScreenConnect back after removal; the RMM is not the root of the intrusion
item.description: Huntress reports several recent incidents in which phishing victims ended up with an MDM client from Hexnode or Rippling followed by an unauthorised ScreenConnect agent. In the Rippling case the attacker used the MDM, running with SYSTEM rights, to stage and run ScreenConnect; in the Hexnode case the managed-service provider removed ScreenConnect and it returned several hours later to the same relay while the Hexnode client was still installed. Huntress says the products are not at fault and that removing the RMM does not remove the management architecture behind it.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Huntress: phished MDM enrolments in Hexnode and Rippling give attackers a management path that brings ScreenConnect back after it has been removed

Huntress reports several recent incidents in which attackers used legitimate mobile-device-management platforms, not flaws in them, as a trusted management path, naming Hexnode and Rippling as the two it saw and noting the list is not definitive (Huntress, 2026-10-28). In the first case, proposal-themed emails led a user to download an MSI named like a DocuSign installer that installed Hexnode components (gateway, agent and PostgreSQL components); ScreenConnect followed shortly after and connected to an attacker relay, the managed-service provider removed it, and it came back several hours later to the same relay while the Hexnode client was still installed (Huntress, 2026-10-28). In the second, a receptionist clicked a link in an email about tax planning that led to a fake Teams calendar page; about a minute later a Rippling enrolment registry key appeared, the agent was downloaded into a SYSTEM profile path and installed with SYSTEM rights, and about 35 minutes after that the attacker used the MDM to stage and run a ScreenConnect installer as SYSTEM (Huntress, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A managed Windows endpoint whose user can run an installer or follow an enrolment link, in an organisation without an inventory of its authorised MDM tenants, agents and RMM instances (Huntress, 2026-10-28).
Detection
The chain Huntress describes as a stronger signal is social engineering, then a new MDM enrolment, then an RMM installation, then outbound communication with an unfamiliar relay, correlated across identity, MDM, endpoint and network telemetry; in endpoint telemetry that is an MSI run from a browser download folder that installs an MDM agent, an enrolment registry key on a device nobody enrolled, a new SYSTEM-level agent in a vendor directory shortly after a click, and an RMM installed by that agent (Huntress, 2026-10-28). A repeat of the same RMM relay after the RMM was removed, as in the Hexnode case, points to a remaining MDM client as a possible source (Huntress, 2026-10-28).

Triage: a corporate enrolment started by IT looks similar in process telemetry; the discriminators are a tenant that is not in the authorised inventory, a trigger that is an emailed link or a user-run installer instead of IT's enrolment workflow, and an RMM install within minutes (an inference from Huntress's two cases).

Defender takeaway
Treat an unexpected MDM enrolment as a security event and keep an inventory of authorised tenants; after removing a rogue RMM, unenrol the device from the unauthorised tenant, disable accounts the attacker created, revoke sessions and tokens, reset credentials and reimage the endpoint if its integrity cannot be confirmed, as Huntress advises (Huntress, 2026-10-28).

item.title: Machelen municipality: foothold from a website's misleading instructions, 22 days to detection; Rhysida lists its files
item.description: The Belgian municipality of Machelen published a timeline in which attackers gained access to an internal laptop through misleading instructions on an external website on 2026-08-20, reached a user with high privileges on 2026-09-10 and were found on 2026-09-11; it confirms that personal data was stolen. Ransomware.live recorded on 2026-10-27 that the Rhysida group had listed the municipal and social-welfare file servers on its leak site, a claim the municipality has not confirmed.
item.content:encoded:
ROUTINENATOA2

Machelen (Belgium) municipality: its own timeline shows a foothold through misleading instructions on an external website on 2026-08-20, found 22 days later after a high-privilege user was reached, with personal data confirmed stolen and Rhysida now listing municipal and social-welfare files

Machelen's own timeline records that on 2026-08-20 attackers gained access to an internal laptop through misleading instructions on an external website, explored it extensively from 24 August to 1 September, and on 10 September had access to a user with high access rights and other IT systems; the municipality found the incident on 11 September, isolated all systems, reported to the Belgian CCB-CERT, restarted part of its systems from a backup of a safe date on 14 September and recorded the first evidence of leaked data on 17 September (Municipality of Machelen, 2026-09-22). It confirms that personal data was leaked and says the scope is still being investigated (Municipality of Machelen, 2026-09-22); the mayor had said on 14 September that no personal data appeared to be affected, and ITdaily reports that this proved wrong (ITdaily, 2026-09-23). Ransomware.live recorded on 2026-10-27 that Rhysida listed Machelen on its leak site, describing the listing as municipal and social-welfare file servers of about 1.3 million files, with client files that include passports and identity cards, nursing-home medical files and civil-status records, which are the group's own claims (Ransomware.live, 2026-10-27).

Detection
The timeline puts 22 days between first access and detection, with the first laptop explored from 24 August to 1 September; it names neither the website nor the commands, so the telemetry to review includes endpoint process creation after a user followed instructions on a web page and later use of a high-privilege account from that workstation, which is an inference from the timeline.
Defender takeaway
Treat a user who followed instructions from a website on a work laptop as a possible intrusion that can sit unseen for weeks; review high-privilege account activity from the user's workstation for the weeks after the event, not only the day it is reported.
